Edomites
EE-dum-ites
n. pl.
From Edom, meaning red, the byname Esau earned over a bowl of red pottage (Genesis 25:30). Their land is the red rock country of Seir, south of the Dead Sea; the Greeks called it Idumea, and it is from that later Idumean line that the Herods came.

Biblical Definition

The Edomites are Esau’s children, and Scripture treats them as the near relation who behaves worst. These are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in mount Seir (Genesis 36:9). The law is remarkably tender toward them: Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother (Deuteronomy 23:7), and Israel was forbidden to take a foot of their land, because Seir was given to Esau as Canaan was given to Jacob. Yet Edom refused Israel passage on the King’s Highway, and the histories record a long enmity: Doeg the Edomite, the herdman of Saul, slaughtered eighty-five priests at Nob when no Israelite would lift a hand (1 Samuel 22:18); Hadad the Edomite was raised up as an adversary to Solomon. The prophets fix Edom’s guilt at one point above all others. When Jerusalem fell, Edom stood in the pass and cheered, and Obadiah’s whole prophecy answers it: For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever (Obadiah 1:10). Ezekiel says the same, that Edom hath dealt against the house of Judah by taking vengeance. Malachi opens with the contrast Paul takes up in Romans 9, and the New Testament closes the account with Herod, an Idumean, seeking the life of the child born King of the Jews.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no EDOMITE entry; the name Edom is defined in the older gazetteers as red, and the Authorized Version’s usage across Genesis, Kings, Chronicles, and the prophets fixes the sense.

expand to see more

EDOMITE, n. — A descendant of Esau, called Edom; an inhabitant of Mount Seir, south and east of the Dead Sea.

The name is from the Hebrew for red, given to Esau at Genesis 25:30 for the red pottage, and answering to the red sandstone of his country.

The Greek and Roman form is Idumean; 1 Maccabees and Josephus use it, and Mark 3:8 has Idumaea.

Webster 1828 does not carry the term; the definition follows Scripture and the standard geographies of Webster’s own century.

Herod the Great was an Idumean by descent, which is why Matthew 2 has an Edomite on the throne when the true Son of David is born.

Key Scripture

Genesis 36:9 — "And these are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in mount Seir:"

Deuteronomy 23:7 — "Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother: thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a stranger in his land."

1 Samuel 22:18 — "And the king said to Doeg, Turn thou, and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned, and he fell upon the priests, and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod."

Obadiah 1:10 — "For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever."

Romans 9:13 — "As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated."

Modern Corruption

Romans 9:13 is the verse most often explained away in the whole New Testament, usually by reducing God’s hatred of Esau to a Hebrew idiom for loving less — a move that empties Paul’s argument of the very thing he is arguing.

expand to see more

The standard evasion says that Esau have I hated is Semitic hyperbole for preference, and that the passage concerns nations rather than persons. Both halves fail. Paul has already anticipated the objection: he raises the choice before the twins were born, neither having done any good or evil, and he states the purpose, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth. He then asks the question no merely national reading would provoke: Is there unrighteousness with God? Nobody asks that about a preference. The doctrine is unconditional election, and the Edomites are its historical illustration — a people descended from Abraham and Isaac, circumcised, near of kin, and passed by.

The other corruption runs opposite, and Christians fall into it more often: using Edom to sanctify grudges. Obadiah condemns Edom for standing in the crossway on the day of his brother’s calamity, for rejoicing over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction. That is a warning against gloating at a brother’s fall, and the Christian who reads Obadiah as permission to relish an enemy’s ruin has read himself into Edom’s part. The law’s own word stands over the whole account: Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother. God judged Edom. He did not hand the judgment over to Jacob.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Edom (H123), red, from adom (H119) to be red; the gentilic is Adomi (H130); the land is Se’ir (H8165), hairy or shaggy, and Greek Idoumaia (G2401).

expand to see more

Hebrew Edom (H123) — red; the byname of Esau (Genesis 25:30) and the name of his nation.

Hebrew adom (H119) — to be red, ruddy; the same root behind Adam and the red earth.

Hebrew Adomi (H130) — Edomite; the gentilic, used of Doeg and of Hadad.

Hebrew Se’ir (H8165) — Seir, the mountain country of Edom, named for its shaggy or wooded slopes.

Greek Idoumaia (G2401) — Idumaea; the later name of the region (Mark 3:8), whence the Herodian house.

Usage

"Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother (Deuteronomy 23:7) — the law’s tenderness toward the nearest enemy."

"Thy violence against thy brother Jacob (Obadiah 1:10) — the single charge on which Edom is condemned."

"Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated (Romans 9:13) — the doctrine of election read out of Edom’s history."
